content: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It poses a significant public health challenge. During childbirth, N. gonorrhoeae can be transmitted from the mother’s genital tract to the newborn, potentially leading to gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum or systemic neonatal infections. In mothers, it can result in complications such as endometritis and pelvic sepsis. This review updates and replaces a previous Cochrane Review on the use of antibiotics to treat gonorrhoea during pregnancy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and potential harms of antibiotics used to treat gonorrhoea in pregnant women. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases and clinical trial registries, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, LILACS, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN Registry, and Epistemonikos. The search included studies published up to April 5, 2017. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different antibiotic regimens for treating gonorrhoea in pregnancy were included, regardless of publication status, language, or country. Trials with cluster or cross-over designs, as well as quasi-RCTs, were excluded. Three review authors independently assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, extracted data, and verified the accuracy of the information. Two RCTs were included in the review, involving a total of 514 pregnant women (347 of whom were analyzed) at an average gestational age of 22 weeks. Both trials were conducted in outpatient settings at two hospitals in the United States between 1993 and 2001, with a follow-up period of 14 days. One of the trials was sponsored by a pharmaceutical company. Both trials were deemed to have a high risk of bias. One trial compared intramuscular ceftriaxone (125 mg) with oral cefixime (400 mg). The other trial had three arms, comparing intramuscular ceftriaxone (250 mg) with either oral amoxicillin (3 g) plus oral probenecid (1 g) or intramuscular spectinomycin (2 g). However, data on spectinomycin were excluded because this medication is no longer manufactured. A meta-analysis could not be performed due to differences in the medications compared across the trials. The evidence was inconclusive regarding differences in the cure rates of gonococcal infections (genital, extragenital, or both) between intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral amoxicillin plus probenecid (risk ratio [RR] 1.07, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.98 to 1.16; one RCT; 168 women; very low-quality evidence) or between intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral cefixime (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.08; one RCT; 95 women; very low-quality evidence). Neither trial reported on key maternal outcomes such as obstetric complications (e.g., miscarriage, premature rupture of membranes, preterm delivery, or fetal death), disseminated gonococcal infection, or neonatal outcomes such as the incidence of ophthalmia neonatorum. One trial documented a single case of vomiting in the group receiving oral amoxicillin plus probenecid. Pain at injection sites was reported but not quantified. Neonates whose mothers were treated with ceftriaxone had a higher frequency of hyperbilirubinemia. No significant differences were observed between groups regarding neonatal malformations. The authors concluded that the reviewed antibiotic regimens achieved high cure rates for gonococcal infections during pregnancy. However, the evidence was inconclusive and did not favor one specific regimen over another. This conclusion was based on very low-quality evidence from two trials, both of which had significant methodological limitations and a high risk of bias. The safety profiles of the antibiotic regimens remain unclear. High-quality RCTs are urgently needed to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and potential harms of antibiotics for treating gonorrhoea in pregnant women. Future trials should adhere to the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) guidelines, follow CONSORT recommendations, and focus on patient-centered outcomes as outlined by the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI).
